--- title: "Storage Backends" description: "Swap graph, vector, and KV storage backends — NetworkX vs SQLite vs Neo4j for graphs, HNSWLib vs NanoVectorDB for vectors." date: today format: html: self-contained: true embed-resources: true code-fold: true code-tools: true --- ## Introduction nano-graphrag uses three types of storage, each with a pluggable backend: | Storage Type | Purpose | Default Backend | Alternatives | |---|---|---|---| | **Graph** | Entity/relationship knowledge graph | `NetworkXStorage` (GraphML files) | `SQLiteGraphStorage`, `Neo4jStorage` | | **Vector** | Entity/chunk similarity search | `HNSWVectorStorage` (hnswlib) | `NanoVectorDBStorage` | | **KV** | Documents, chunks, community reports | `JsonKVStorage` (JSON files) | — | Backends are configured by passing the storage class to the `GraphRAG` constructor. All backends implement the same async interface, so you can swap them without changing any application logic. This notebook demonstrates: 1. **Default setup** (NetworkX + HNSWLib) 2. **SQLite graph backend** — persistent, WAL-mode SQLite database 3. **NanoVectorDB** — lightweight pure-Python vector store 4. **Neo4j** — configuration for production graph databases (requires a running Neo4j server) 5. **Backend comparison** — when to use each ## Setup ::: {#setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import logging import os import time from pathlib import Path logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING) logging.getLogger("nano-graphrag").setLevel(logging.INFO) TEXT_SNIPPET = ( "Alice works at Wonderland Labs as a quantum researcher. " "Bob is the CTO of Wonderland Labs and oversees the AI division. " "Carol founded DataForge, a startup building graph databases. " "Dave joined DataForge as lead engineer after leaving CloudCorp. " "Eve is a security consultant who audits both Wonderland Labs and DataForge." ) ``` ::: ::: {#imports .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} from nano_graphrag import GraphRAG, QueryParam from nano_graphrag._storage import ( HNSWVectorStorage, NetworkXStorage, SQLiteGraphStorage, ) ``` ::: ## 1. Default: NetworkX + HNSWLib The default backend stores the graph as a GraphML XML file and vectors in an hnswlib index. This is ideal for development and small-to-medium datasets. ::: {#default-setup .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} WORKING_DIR_DEFAULT = Path("./_cache/04_storage_backends/default") WORKING_DIR_DEFAULT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) rag_default = GraphRAG( working_dir=str(WORKING_DIR_DEFAULT), ) print(f"Graph backend: {rag_default.graph_storage_cls.__name__}") print(f"Vector backend: {rag_default.vector_db_storage_cls.__name__}") print(f"KV backend: {rag_default.key_string_value_json_storage_cls.__name__}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

SQLite Graph Backend `SQLiteGraphStorage` stores the graph in a SQLite database with WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode. It supports the same Leiden clustering algorithm via an in-memory NetworkX projection. **Advantages over NetworkX:** - **Atomic writes** — SQLite transactions prevent data corruption on crash - **Better concurrency** — WAL mode allows concurrent reads during writes - **Scalability** — handles larger graphs without loading everything into memory - **Portable** — single `.db` file, easy to backup and transfer ::: {#sqlite-setup .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} WORKING_DIR_SQLITE = Path("./_cache/04_storage_backends/sqlite") WORKING_DIR_SQLITE.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) rag_sqlite = GraphRAG( working_dir=str(WORKING_DIR_SQLITE), graph_storage_cls=SQLiteGraphStorage, ) print(f"Graph backend: {rag_sqlite.graph_storage_cls.__name__}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

NanoVectorDB Backend `NanoVectorDBStorage` is a lightweight pure-Python vector database that stores vectors in a JSON file. It's a good alternative when you don't want the hnswlib C dependency. **Advantages over HNSWLib:** - **Pure Python** — no native C extensions, works everywhere (including WASM) - **Simple** — single JSON file, easy to inspect and debug - **Portable** — no platform-specific binaries **Trade-offs:** - Slower search on large datasets (brute-force cosine similarity) - Higher memory usage for large vector collections ::: {#check-nanovectordb .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} try: from nano_graphrag._storage import NanoVectorDBStorage HAS_NANOVEC = True print("NanoVectorDB available") except Exception: HAS_NANOVEC = False print("NanoVectorDB not installed (pip install nano-vectordb)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` NanoVectorDB available ``` ::: ::: ::: {#nanovecdb-setup .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} if HAS_NANOVEC: WORKING_DIR_NANOVEC = Path("./_cache/04_storage_backends/nanovecdb") WORKING_DIR_NANOVEC.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) rag_nanovec = GraphRAG( working_dir=str(WORKING_DIR_NANOVEC), vector_db_storage_cls=NanoVectorDBStorage, ) print(f"Vector backend: {rag_nanovec.vector_db_storage_cls.__name__}") start = time.time() await rag_nanovec.ainsert(TEXT_SNIPPET) elapsed = time.time() - start print(f"Insert complete in {elapsed:.1f}s") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

Best for prototyping, notebooks, and datasets under ~100K edges. - **SQLite** — Step up when you need crash safety, atomic writes, or have graphs with 100K+ edges. - **Neo4j** — Production deployments with multi-user access, complex graph queries, or very large graphs. **When to choose which vector backend:** - **HNSWLib** — Default. Fast approximate nearest neighbor search. Best for most use cases. - **NanoVectorDB** — When you need pure Python (no C extensions), e.g., WASM environments or restricted deployment targets. ## Summary In this notebook we: - **Default**: Used NetworkX + HNSWLib (zero-config storage) - **SQLite graph**: Swapped to `SQLiteGraphStorage` for atomic, crash-safe graph persistence - **NanoVectorDB**: Swapped to `NanoVectorDBStorage` for a pure-Python vector backend - **Neo4j**: Showed configuration for production-grade graph database (requires server) - **Mixed**: Demonstrated combining SQLite graph + NanoVectorDB in a single instance - **Compared** all backends by storage format, execution model, and ideal use case Next up: [Extraction Pipeline](05-extraction-pipeline.md) — structured vs legacy extraction, GLiNER, and quality modes.
